The day's crypto news is a mixture of market positioning, fund flows, policy updates, and company decisions. The headlines below are worth reading for the detail behind them, not just the reaction on a price chart.

What is moving the conversation

Live news: Bitcoin briefly drops below 200-week moving average. Bitcoin fell below its 200-week moving average as the Dollar Index held above 103, while gold struggled to recover and oil prices rebounded. Readers should check the original report before treating the headline as a confirmed change in the market.

Ethereum treasury firm BTCS sold ether at a loss to keep $64 million Aave loan healthy. The Nasdaq-listed company has 46,676 ETH backing its borrowings, and the loan could become eligible for liquidation if ether slides to around $1,700. Readers should check the original report before treating the headline as a confirmed change in the market.

Bitcoin firm Nakamoto owes Kraken $165 million, more than its entire market value. About 70% of the bitcoin treasury firm’s coins are pledged to the exchange, bought at roughly $118,000 each, and bitcoin now trades under $69,000. Readers should check the original report before treating the headline as a confirmed change in the market.

Bitcoin ETFs are now down over $1.5 billion in net outflows for the year. Recent rapid redemptions explain the market swoon. Bitcoin's spot price fell below $70,000 on Friday, the lowest since August. Readers should check the original report before treating the headline as a confirmed change in the market.

SpaceX-Tesla merger talks put 30,000 bitcoin back in focus. A deal could be announced as soon as December, putting $2.1 billion of bitcoin under one roof, a sliver of what the combined group would be worth. Readers should check the original report before treating the headline as a confirmed change in the market.

Bitcoin dips below $70,000 as Dollar Index hits 19-month high. The crypto market selloff gathered pace early Friday. Bitcoin dropped below $70,000 and ether traded below $2,000, triggering large liquidations in futures market. Readers should check the original report before treating the headline as a confirmed change in the market.

Market context

Bitcoin is around $69,362 with a -5.35% 24-hour move, while Ether is around $1,953.61 with a -4.27% move. Those figures are a snapshot, not a forecast. The useful question is whether the move is supported by spot demand, volume, and a clear change in the news.

When the market is quiet, leverage and liquidity can matter as much as direction. A small headline can move price quickly when traders are positioned too closely on one side.

What to watch next

  • New ETF creations and redemptions.
  • Futures open interest and funding rates.
  • Fresh regulatory text or official statements.
  • Security warnings, outages, or custody changes.
  • Whether the reported developments become live products rather than announcements.

The fairest reading today is cautious attention. There are real developments in the industry, but none should be stretched into a guaranteed market direction.

items.description:

## Bitcoin ETFs Post First Weekly Inflows Since May [...] Daily flows reflected continued uncertainty among investors. Funds attracted more than $265 million on July 6, the strongest single-day inflow since early May, before sharply slowing the following day.

The middle of the week saw renewed outflows before demand recovered again on Friday with another positive session.

Despite the improvement, the latest inflows remain small compared with the more than $8 billion that exited Bitcoin ETFs over the previous eight weeks. [...] US-listed spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $197.4 million in net inflows during the week ending July 10, breaking an eight-week streak of outflows that had persisted since the second week of May.

The weekly figure was driven primarily by BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT), which continued to dominate the market.

IBIT attracted nearly $292 million during the week, offsetting significant withdrawals from Grayscale's GBTC, Fidelity's FBTC, and ARK 21Shares' Bitcoin ETF.

items.title: Stablecoins just got the regulatory clarity industry wanted
items.description:
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) finalized rules for implementing the landmark stablecoin legislation President Trump signed into law last year, known as the GENIUS Act. Those rules ease several proposed restrictions on how stablecoin issuers must manage their reserves, including a previous maturity limit that would have prevented issuers from holding longer-term Treasurys.

The OCC, meanwhile, left one of the biggest industry disputes over stablecoins unanswered. [...] While the GENIUS Act prevents stablecoin issuers from paying interest directly, the OCC eliminated a proposed provision that would have barred crypto exchanges and other third-party platforms from offering customers yield on their idle stablecoin balances.

Instead, the agency said it will evaluate those kinds of arrangements on an individual basis.

Read more:How to start buying crypto for $100 [...] Circle Internet Group (CRCL), the country's largest stablecoin issuer, and major crypto exchange Coinbase Global (COIN) applauded the new rules. (Disclosure: Yahoo Finance has a partnership with Coinbase.)

"We welcome the OCC's final rules implementing the GENIUS Act — an important milestone in translating America's leadership on stablecoin legislation into clear, durable regulatory standards," Dante Disparte, Circle's chief strategy officer and head of global policy, said in a statement.

items.description:
Cryptocurrency regulation is no longer a theoretical debate—it’s an evolving framework that is beginning to take shape worldwide. In the United States, Congress has moved toward establishing federal oversight of stablecoins and digital asset markets. The GENIUS Act, signed into law in 2025, established a federal regulatory framework for stablecoins, while broader market structure legislation known as the CLARITY Act advanced in Congress in 2026 but has yet to become law. [...] The GENIUS Act, signed into law in 2025, established the first federal regulatory framework for stablecoins in the United States. It limits who can issue stablecoins and requires issuers to maintain reserves backing the tokens they have issued, make monthly disclosures detailing the assets held in reserve, and comply with anti–money laundering and consumer protection requirements.

items.title: Why stablecoins are quickly becoming a geopolitical issue | World Economic Forum
items.description: The currency composition of the market adds another layer of international relevance. Most major stablecoins are pegged to the US dollar, which means their spread can extend the dollar’s reach through new digital channels. In that sense, stablecoins are not only payment tools. They are also part of the evolving infrastructure of international monetary influence. If digital transactions increasingly rely on dollar-linked tokens, then dollar power may become more deeply embedded in the [...] This is one reason stablecoins now sit at the intersection of efficiency and vulnerability. They can reduce friction in cross-border money movement and widen access to dollar liquidity. At the same time, they can reduce the policy space available to countries that are already economically exposed. Their geopolitical significance comes from that tension. They promise useful infrastructure, yet they can also redistribute monetary influence in ways that favor the issuers of dominant currencies and [...] Stablecoins increasingly touch cross-border payments, the international role of the dollar, the resilience of financial infrastructure and the policy autonomy of states. That combination has turned them into a geopolitical issue; they exist at the intersection of technology, money and power now meet.

items.title: De-dollarization: The End of Dollar Dominance?
items.description:
All things considered, suggestions of the dollar’s demise are premature — at least for now. The greenback still anchors global reserves, payments, financing and FX trading, reinforced by the depth of U.S. capital markets and a lack of viable alternatives. However, future geopolitical developments could accelerate a move toward a more multipolar monetary system — one in which the dollar remains dominant, but other currencies play increasingly larger roles.

## Related insights [...] The dollar-centric system gives the U.S. significant geopolitical leverage beyond cheaper funding costs, including the ability to impose sanctions, shape access to key payment channels and obtain visibility into transactions between third countries that clear flows through U.S.-linked infrastructure. However, this is gradually eroding as more countries learn to route around sanctions and invest in domestic and alternative cross-border payment rails. [...] September 04, 2026
